title: Berkshire 2015: float as a revolving fund, owning part of great businesses, and never betting against America
summary: Buffett's 2015 letter explains why Berkshire's intrinsic value outruns book value, how insurance float and underwriting discipline create value, and why a partial stake in a wonderful company beats owning all of a mediocre one. It also covers honest accounting (stock comp, EBITDA, amortization), productivity and the long-run case for America.

principles.text: Under GAAP, winners are never written up, so intrinsic value diverges from book value; buy back shares at a discount to intrinsic value.
principles.quote: That’s why we would be delighted to repurchase our shares should they sell as low as 120% of book value. At that level, purchases would instantly and meaningfully increase per-share intrinsic value for Berkshire’s continuing shareholders.

principles.text: Prefer a partial stake in a wonderful business over full ownership of a so-so one.
principles.quote: At Berkshire, we much prefer owning a non-controlling but substantial portion of a wonderful company to owning 100% of a so-so business. It’s better to have a partial interest in the Hope Diamond than to own all of a rhinestone.

principles.text: Float is a revolving fund, not strictly a liability; if costless and long-enduring it is worth far more than its accounting treatment.
principles.quote: But to think of float as strictly a liability is incorrect. It should instead be viewed as a revolving fund.

principles.text: Sound insurance requires willingness to walk away when the right premium can't be had; copying competitors is the classic failure.
principles.quote: Many insurers pass the first three tests and flunk the fourth. They simply can’t turn their back on business that is being eagerly written by their competitors.

principles.text: A durable low-cost advantage is a moat that competitors cannot cross, letting a company take share year after year.
principles.quote: The company’s low costs create a moat – an enduring one – that competitors are unable to cross.

principles.text: Stock-based compensation is a real expense; ignoring it, or leaning on EBITDA, misleads investors.
principles.quote: “Stock-based compensation” is the most egregious example. The very name says it all: “compensation.” If compensation isn’t an expense, what is it?
